title: No-tracking reads, SQL logs, tags and interceptors
summary: Read without tracking, see the SQL EF sends, label it with TagWith, recognise N+1 in a log, and hook into every command or save with an interceptor.

steps.title: Reads that do not track
body: By default every entity a query returns is **tracked**: the context keeps a snapshot of it to detect changes at `SaveChanges`. That costs memory and CPU, and a read-only endpoint never saves. Say so:
- A projection with `Select(o => new OrderDto(...))` is never tracked anyway, and usually the best read: only the columns you need.
- `AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution()` does not track but still returns the same object for the same row (useful with `Include`).
- A context used only for queries can default to it: `options.UseQueryTrackingBehavior(QueryTrackingBehavior.NoTracking)`.
Keep tracking when you load an entity in order to change and save it: that is what change tracking is for.

steps.prompt: How many entities is the context tracking after each query?
code: db.Customers.AddRange(new Customer { Name = "Ana" }, new Customer { Name = "Ben" });
protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options.UseSqlite("Data Source=shop.db");
steps.explain: The no-tracking query leaves the change tracker empty. The normal query tracks the one customer it returned.

steps.title: See the SQL: LogTo and TagWith
body: Never guess what EF sends. In development, log it:

In an ASP.NET Core app the same events also flow into normal logging: set `"Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command": "Information"` in `appsettings.Development.json`. For one query, `query.ToQueryString()` returns the SQL without running it.

In production, the SQL shows up in the database's own tools (`pg_stat_statements`, Query Store, slow-query logs), where nobody knows which endpoint sent it. **`TagWith`** puts a comment at the top of the SQL that travels with it:

steps.prompt: What are the first two lines `ToQueryString()` returns for this query?
code: var sql = db.Orders.TagWith("dashboard: big orders").Where(o => o.TotalCents > 10000).ToQueryString();
protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options.UseSqlite("Data Source=shop.db");
steps.explain: The tag becomes a SQL comment, followed by a blank line, then the query. Tags have no effect on the plan; they only make the query findable.

steps.title: N+1, as it looks in the log
body: Support says the customer summary page takes 6 seconds. The development log shows this, and much more of the same:

The fingerprint of **N+1**: one query for the list, then the **same** query with a different parameter, once per row. Each is fast; thousands of round trips are not. (`@c_Id='?'` is how EF logs parameters without `EnableSensitiveDataLogging`.)
The fix is to ask for everything in one query: a projection that lets the database count and sum per customer, or `Include` when you need whole entities.

steps.prompt: A request logs 1 query for 200 orders, then 200 queries `SELECT ... FROM "Customers" WHERE "c"."Id" = @p`. Which change fixes it best for a page that shows order id, total and customer name?
options: Project in one query: `db.Orders.Select(o => new { o.Id, o.TotalCents, Customer = o.Customer!.Name })`
Wrap the loop in a transaction
Turn on `AsNoTracking()` for the customer queries
Cache each customer in a `Dictionary` inside the loop
steps.explain: The projection becomes one SQL query with a JOIN and returns only the three columns the page shows. A dictionary only helps when customers repeat, and still sends one query per distinct customer.

steps.title: Fix the slow summary
prompt: `GET /customers/summary` returns each customer's **name**, number of **orders** and **totalCents**, sorted by name. It is correct but runs one query per customer, exactly like the log in the card.

Rewrite it as **one** query: a `Select` projection into `CustomerSummary` that counts and sums `c.Orders` in the database. Tag it with `TagWith("customer summary")` so it can be found in production. **Run checks** starts your server and calls it.
template: public static async Task Run(HttpClient http)
foreach (var dojoName in new[] { "Ben", "Ana", "Chloe", "Dmitri" }) await http.PostAsJsonAsync("/customers", new { name = dojoName });
foreach (var (dojoC, dojoT) in new[] { (1, 3000), (2, 4500), (2, 900), (3, 1200), (2, 600) }) await http.PostAsJsonAsync("/orders", new { customerId = dojoC, totalCents = dojoT });

var dojoRows = dojoJson.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.Array ? string.Join("|", dojoJson.EnumerateArray().Select(x => $"{DojoWeb.Prop(x, "name")} {DojoWeb.Prop(x, "orders")} {DojoWeb.Prop(x, "totalCents")}")) : "(not an array)";
Dojo.Check("...in one SQL command, however many customers", DojoSql.Commands == 1, $"it ran {DojoSql.Commands} commands");
Dojo.Check("...tagged \"customer summary\" in the SQL", dojoFirst.StartsWith("-- customer summary"), "the SQL starts with: " + dojoFirst.Split('\n')[0]);
if (e.Value is CommandExecutedEventData d) lock (Log) Log.Add(d.Command.CommandText);
hints: `c.Orders.Count` and `c.Orders.Sum(o => o.TotalCents)` inside the Select become SQL subqueries or a join.
steps.explain: One round trip, however many customers, and the DBA can find it by its tag. Dmitri, with no orders, gets 0 and 0: the projection handles the empty case that a JOIN plus GROUP BY written by hand often gets wrong.

steps.title: Interceptors: code that runs on every command or save
body: An **interceptor** hooks into EF's pipeline for every context it is registered on. Common real uses: log commands slower than a threshold, stamp audit columns on save, set a session variable for row-level security.
CommandExecutedEventData data, DbDataReader result, CancellationToken ct = default)
if (e.State is EntityState.Added or EntityState.Modified) e.Entity.UpdatedAt = DateTime.UtcNow;

Every hook has a sync and an async version (`SavingChanges` / `SavingChangesAsync`). The default async one does **not** call the sync one, so override both, or code that calls `SaveChanges()` skips your audit.

steps.title: An audit interceptor
prompt: Write `class AuditInterceptor(string user) : SaveChangesInterceptor` that, before every save, goes through the tracked `Note` entries and:
- for **Added** and **Modified** notes, sets `ChangedBy` to `user` and adds 1 to `Revision`;

Override **both** `SavingChanges` and `SavingChangesAsync`, so `SaveChanges()` and `SaveChangesAsync()` are both audited. Each returns the `result` it was given (`ValueTask.FromResult(result)` in the async one).
`Note` (`Id`, `Text`, `ChangedBy`, `Revision`) and `NotesDb` are given; the tests register your interceptor with `AddInterceptors`.
solution: public override InterceptionResult<int> SavingChanges(DbContextEventData eventData, InterceptionResult<int> result)
template: Dojo.Eq("SaveChanges() on an added note sets ChangedBy", "api", dojoNote.ChangedBy);
Dojo.Eq("...the unchanged note is not touched by the second save", "doors at 19:30", dojoNotes[0].Text);
hints: `context.ChangeTracker.Entries<Note>()` gives each tracked note with its `State`.
Put the loop in a private method and call it from both overrides; the async one returns `ValueTask.FromResult(result)`.
steps.explain: The same pattern stamps `UpdatedAt` and `UpdatedBy` on every entity implementing an `IAudited` interface. In a real app the user comes from an injected service reading `HttpContext.User`, and the time from an injected `TimeProvider` so tests can control it.
